'''John Markus Blatt''' (23 November 1921, Vienna – 16 March 1990, [[Haifa]]) was an Austrian-born American theoretical physicist.

==Life==
Blatt was the son of a successful physician in Vienna. In 1938 the family immigrated to the US as Jews fleeing the [[Anschluss]]. Blatt studied physics at the [[University of Cincinnati]] with bachelor's degree in 1942 and received in 1946 two doctorates in physics, one from [[Cornell University]] and the other from [[Princeton University]]. He then went to [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where he wrote, with [[Victor Weisskopf]], the textbook ''Theoretical Nuclear Physics'', which became a standard introduction to the subject. From 1948 to 1953 Blatt was at the [[University of Illinois]], where the [[Illiac]] computer was being built. Blatt was involved in the project and became a pioneer in the use of computers in theoretical nuclear physics. During the McCarthy era, he was dissatisfied with the political climate in the United States and immigrated to Australia, where in 1953 he joined the faculty of the [[University of Sydney]].<ref name=PT/> There, in collaboration with [[Max Robert Schafroth]] (1923–1959)<ref name="Butler1959">{{cite journal |last1=Butler |first1=S. T. |year=1959 |title=Dr. M. R. Schafroth |journal=Nature |volume=184 |issue=4684 |pages=403–404 |bibcode=1959Natur.184..403B |doi=10.1038/184403b0 |issn=0028-0836 |doi-access=free}} Max Robert Schafroth was a Swiss physicist and student and assistant of [[Wolfgang Pauli]] in Zürich. In 1954, Schafroth moved to Australia to work at the University of Sydney. He was killed in May 1959 in the crash of a small airplane.</ref> and [[Stuart Thomas Butler]], he developed a theory that explained [[superconductivity]] as a [[Bose-Einstein condensate|Bose-Einstein condensation]] of electron pairs.<ref name=PT>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.2809506|title=John M. Blatt|journal=Physics Today|volume=45|issue=1|pages=84|year=1992|last1=Blatt|first1=Frank J.|bibcode=1992PhT....45a..84B|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Schafroth, M. R.|author2=Butler, S. T.|author3=Blatt, J. M.|title=Quasichemical equilibrium approach to superconductivity|journal=Helvetica Physica Acta |year=1957|volume=30|pages=93–134|url=https://www.e-periodica.ch/digbib/view?pid=hpa-001:1957:30::95#95}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m2sLGjfXyxwC&pg=PA134|title = A Career in Theoretical Physics|isbn = 9789810217181|last1 = Anderson|first1 = Philip W.|year = 1994|pages=134–135}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=m2sLGjfXyxwC&pg=PA135 p. 135]</ref>

{{blockquote|Blatt, Butler, and Schafroth rejected [[BCS theory|BCS]] for a number of years, offering an alternative in the summer of 1957. This "quasi-chemical approach" expanded on Schafroth's earlier theory of superconductivity as a Bose-Einstein condensation of pairs of electrons.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-2vmCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA559|title = Out of the Crystal Maze: Chapters from the History of Solid State Physics|isbn = 9780195053296|last1 = Hoddeson|first1 = Lillian|last2 = Braun|first2 = Ernst|last3 = Teichmann|first3 = Jurgen|last4 = Weart|first4 = Spencer R.|year = 1992|page=559}}</ref>}}

Together with [[Takeo Matsubara]], Blatt later proved that the quasi-chemical theory and the [[BCS theory]] were equivalent.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Blatt |first1=J.M. |title=Electron pairs in the theory of superconductivity |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics |year=1960 |volume=23 |issue=3|page=447—450}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Matsubara |first1=Takeo |last2=Blatt |first2=J.M. |title=Bose Einstein condensation of correlated pairs |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics |year=1960 |volume=23 |issue=3|page=451—474}}</ref>  

Blatt's energetic and argumentative personality led to conflict at the University of Sydney, so in 1959 he became a professor of applied mathematics at the newly founded [[University of New South Wales]], where he remained until his retirement in 1984. During the 1960s he published ''Theory of Superconductivity'' (1964), two books on [[FORTRAN]] programming, and, in collaboration with S. B. Butler, two introductory physics textbooks. During his career at the University of New South Wales, he dealt with the three-body nuclear problem, statistical mechanics and applied mathematics such as the theory of optimal control. He brought a number of important mathematicians to the university such as [[George Szekeres]] and ensured that computer science teaching was expanded and students were trained early on computers. In the later part of his career, he worked on mathematical economics.<ref name=Franklin>{{cite journal|title=Profile of a Mathematician: John Blatt|last=Franklin|first=James|author-link=James Franklin (philosopher)|journal=Parabola|volume=37|issue=2|year=2001|pages=15–17|url=https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~jim/blatt.html}}</ref> He published over 100 articles.<ref name=PT/>

Blatt was an accomplished amateur pianist.<ref name=Franklin/>

==Family==
Blatt married Sylvia Epstein in 1945; they divorced in 1967. He married his second wife, Ruth Ne'eman, in 1971.<ref name="RöderStrauss2016">{{cite book|editor1=Röder, Werner|editor2=Strauss, Herbert A.|title=Biographisches Handbuch der deutschsprachigen Emigration nach 1933–1945|volume=II|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eNKJDwAAQBAJ&pg=RA1-PA115|year=1999|publisher=De Gruyter|isbn=978-3-11-096854-5|page=115}}</ref> He and his second wife retired to Haifa in 1984. He remained scientifically active there and taught at the University of Haifa. From his first marriage, he had four children, two of whom became computer scientists.<ref name=Franklin/>
